claims.text: Architecture governance is how an organisation makes sure architecture decisions are taken by the right people, recorded and followed; lightweight governance does it with a few written rules instead of an approval step for every change.
claims.source_hint: glossary architecture-governance; outline item 1; docs/team/architecture-governance.md @ stage-4 lines 3-6

claims.text: architecture-governance.md: the team has no separate architecture approval step per change; most changes need only an ordinary pull request review, the rest an ADR following docs/adr/README.md; no separate architecture review board.

A principle in architecture-governance.md is a short rule drawn from decisions already made, with its reason and what it implies; NT1-NT5 each list reason, implication and source (NT1: data-ownership.md, ADR 0002, 0003; NT5: ADR 0011).

NT1: each service owns its data, no service reads or writes another's tables; reason: with exactly one owner you know whom to trust when copies disagree; implication: ask via a call or message, or keep a copy with a stated way to update.
ADR 0011 (not wrapping RabbitMQ behind a neutral layer) has status Bị từ chối (Rejected) in docs/adr/README.md.
claims.source_hint: docs/adr/README.md @ stage-4, Danh sách table row 0011

claims.text: Decision-rights table rows: change inside a module/service without contract change → the person doing it via ordinary PR review, no ADR, ask the PR reviewer (example: split a class in Payments, change how Catalog reads cache).

Changing a public API or message contract (e.g. dropping a field of POST /api/v1/orders) → team lead after the comment period, ADR, ask the owner of each side reading that contract (app, receiving service).
Changing shop data, permissions, keys or a trust boundary → team lead, ADR checked against threat-model.md, ask the platform developer and the product owner if shops can see it.

Self-run component, vendor or paid service → team lead with product owner (answers for what the product offers shops), ADR with an evaluation like payment-gateway-evaluation.md (payment gateway comparison), ask the product owner; line 27 asks the product owner when its change is visible to shops.

claims.text: Departing from a principle (example: a service reading another service's table for a time) → team lead, ADR recording the exception and when to review it, ask whoever owns the affected part.

Automatic checks in fitness-functions.md run on every change; backend-review-checklist.md is used when a backend design change is reviewed (PR with ADR/design doc, or touching a boundary, data, limits), cluster-review-checklist.md when a cluster change is reviewed.

claims.text: The decision-rights table is reviewed when there are several teams, because 'the owner of the reading side' may then be another team.

Each exception is an ADR recording the principle departed from, the reason and a review deadline, listed in the Ngoại lệ section so rule and exception are seen together; at stage-4 the table lists no exception.

Trade-offs: a board approving every design adds a wait to every change; principles + decision rights + checks put a person's time only where an ADR is needed; writing nothing is fast but an unwritten rule is easy to break unnoticed. Each fits a stated context.

When a principle can be stated exactly enough for a machine, leave it to the check (a contract change itself still takes its ADR); when a kind of change is costly and no check sees it, give it its own ADR row; when a second team appears, look at the decision-rights table again.
A principle without its reason is hard to apply to an unforeseen case; writing exceptions as ADRs with a review date keeps the rule and its exceptions visible.

Try it: Catalog cache change → ordinary PR, no ADR; drop a field of POST /api/v1/orders → team lead, ADR, ask the app's owner; Payments reading a Notifications table → NT1 exception ADR, listed under Ngoại lệ; paid SMS service → team lead + product owner, ADR with evaluation.
